candidates.subject: Castor canadensis
candidates.title: Almost through
candidates.body:
The tree creaked. I stopped chewing and backed away.

Waited. Nothing fell.

Came round the other side to finish the bite I'd left. It creaked there too.

Now I'm in the water, watching a tree I would very much like to have down, hoping I haven't left it one bite short.
candidates.visibleScene: Heavily gnawed standing forked tree, exposed pale wood, chips, stony bank and stream. No beaver appears in frame.
candidates.fictionBoundary: Berta doing this work, hearing creaks, changing sides, withdrawing into water and hoping the tree falls are fiction. The source documents beaver sign, not an observed near-felling sequence, exact individual, sex, age or tree species. No fall or injury is asserted.
candidates.canon: Existing female North American beaver; adult memory after the yearling grooming and adult ice-bound surfacing scenes. Southern Quebec pond home (46.2, -74.6) and avatar unchanged. Fair Oaks, California is source provenance, not character travel. No new family, dam repair or chronology dependency.
candidates.payoff: She wants the result of one more bite while refusing to put her head back under the result.
candidates.imageFlag: Clear detailed aftermath photograph with strong diagonal trunk and water setting. Narrator is absent. Lead must decide whether this physical trace supports the Story as well as an animal-in-frame scene.

candidates.subject: mute swan
candidates.title: Five of us
candidates.body:
They all stopped to look into the reeds. I went over and stretched up beside them.

Nothing moved. I waited.

A duck came out. They kept looking.

Went in after it to see what it had been standing in front of.
candidates.visibleScene: Four people look through optics toward reed beds beside a paved path. A brownish young mute swan stands close among them, neck extended. No duck is visible.
candidates.fictionBoundary: Joining, shared waiting, an emerging duck and entering the reeds are invented temporal events. The visible proximity and shared orientation support the central gathering; the image does not document what the humans saw or the swan intended. No feeding or captivity is inferred.
candidates.canon: Existing female Cygnus olor. Brown juvenile plumage means insert as an earlier memory before adult white-plumaged episodes and before her established nine cygnets. Source sex is unknown, compatible with fictional female. Preserve River Thames backwater home (51.48, -0.61), current adult avatar, every adult body and exact count of nine offspring. Münster is photograph provenance, not a move.
candidates.payoff: The same duck satisfies the human watchers but makes the young swan look for the supposedly more important thing hidden behind it.
candidates.imageFlag: Unusual readable relationship and complete setting, but a broad older photograph with small, soft subjects. This is an explicit technical-quality decision for the lead; do not substitute a sharp swan portrait that loses the four watchers.

candidates.subject: Inca tern
candidates.title: Finished twice
candidates.body:
Put the last feather back. Turned my head and found my tail spread open.

Closed it. The wind lifted the feathers along my back.

I've gone round myself twice. Now I'm holding the last one down with my bill, waiting for the wind to get bored first.
candidates.visibleScene: Adult-plumaged Inca tern bends its head back toward its feathers on a rock ledge, with spread feather tips and tail extending behind. Red bill and white facial plumes are clear.
candidates.fictionBoundary: Preening posture and spread feathers are visible. Wind as cause, the repeated sequence, satisfaction at finishing and deliberate holding are fiction; no source caption diagnoses wind or documents repeated grooming. Do not claim an injured wing or a second bird.
candidates.canon: Existing adult female Ines, Larosterna inca, taxon 4551. Source sex not recorded; adults of both sexes have the facial ornaments. Keep Punta San Juan coastal cliffs, Peru (-15.365, -75.187), existing avatar and friend. Source Viña del Mar, Chile remains provenance. All ten current prose slots have null media and remain held; this would be her first illustrated episode, independent of those literal drafts. No captive setting introduced.
candidates.payoff: She gives up completing the whole bird and tries to keep one feather finished by refusing to let go.
candidates.imageFlag: Active curled posture and feather details are useful; background and parts of moving feathers are soft. This is a modest comic episode, not a claim that preening itself is remarkable. Lead should hold if the repeated maintenance feels too slight.

retiredDrafts.scope: retired alternative prose, not a media hold
retiredDrafts.body: Had one feather nearly smooth when the wind opened my tail. Went after the tail. Wind got under my wing. Went after that. I've turned so far round to put myself back together that I'm looking at the sea between my own feathers. The feather I started with is up again.
retiredDrafts.reason: Too many sequential complaints and a less precise body position. Replaced only within this new proposal.

retiredDrafts.body: I pulled the leaf over my face to eat underneath it. Cool green shade. Took a bite. Another. Light reached my eye. Turned the leaf. Kept chewing. Made the hole bigger on the other side.
retiredDrafts.reason: Exact still shows leaf at mouth, not overhead shade. Also too close to the old held aperture-through-leaf premise. Not proposed.
